title: Tractatus
author: Maximus of Turin
source: Translated by Claude from tmp912.tmp912.opp-lat1, as held by Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina.
statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.

passages.original: et nihil a fato petebant, sed totum, ut dixi, sinceritate 723 fidei et divinis opibus, et miserationibus adimplebant. Fato dicis omnia fieri? Sed stultus stulta loquitur, et cor ejus vana intelligit, et, sicut ille aiebat Tullius in Horlensio dicens : Aria mea dicebat hoc quod dicis, fato omnia fieri; mater autem mulier sapiens non existimavit. Et nos possumus dicere in veritate, quia avia nostra, id est error antiquus et genlilis stultitia hoc dicebal.
passages.english: and they sought nothing from fate, but, as I have said, they accomplished everything by the sincerity of faith, by divine resources, and by acts of mercy. Do you say that all things happen by fate? But the fool speaks foolish things, and his heart understands vain things; and, as that Tully said in the Hortensius: "My grandmother used to say what you say, that all things happen by fate; but my mother, a wise woman, did not think so." And we can say in truth that our grandmother, that is, ancient error and gentile folly, used to say this.
passages.notes: Scanning errors corrected: 'Horlensio' = Hortensio, 'Aria' = Avia (grandmother, confirmed by 'avia nostra'), 'genlilis' = gentilis, 'dicebal' = dicebat. The marginal number 723 is omitted.

passages.original: Hic, cum vesano furore raperetur, filios devoravit suos; qui et operto capite, ne agnosceretur, effugit et ita in delubris vestris formatur. Jovem ejus filium a matre subtractum insula habet sepulcrum... despectus jacet..... unde Virgilius dixit: cremedio jacet insulade criminibus.... breviter commemorat dicens : 3 Jovisque et soror, et conjux, et rapti, inquit, Ganymedis honores. Viic quam exsecrabilis habendus sit, imo potius quam detestabilis iste Jupiter, qui sororem voluerit habere uxorem, ut de cæteris ejus criminibus taceamus.
passages.english: He, when he was seized by a mad frenzy, devoured his own sons; and he fled with his head covered so as not to be recognised, and so he is portrayed in your shrines. Jupiter his son, taken away [to safety] by his mother, has a tomb on an island... he lies despised..... whence Virgil said: ... ... the island lies ... for crimes.... He briefly mentions [this], saying: "and Jove's sister and wife, and the honours," he says, "of ravished Ganymede." See how accursed, or rather how detestable, this Jupiter must be held, who wanted to have his sister as wife, to say nothing of his other crimes.
passages.notes: The text is lacunose. 'cremedio jacet insulade criminibus' is corrupt and cannot be construed; only fragments are rendered. The Virgil quotation conflates Aeneid 1.47 and 1.28. 'Viic' is read as 'Vide' (see). The footnote numeral 3 is omitted.

passages.original: 1 Ergo nunc Dominum Deum nostrum velint nolit' et ipsi philosophi veritate compressi, et invisibilem asserunt, et omnium praepotentem, in quo præcipuus Sostenes formam hujus mundi negat conspici posse, et angelos veros sedi ejus dicit assistere, in quo et Plato pari ratione consentit, et unum Deum prædicans, Ceteros angelos vel daemones dicit. Hermes quoque Trismegistus unum Deum fatetur, eumque inviaibilem 730 atque incomprehensibilem confiletur. Hunc ergo nos in veritate confitemur, et novimus, et fatemur.
passages.english: So now, whether they will or not, even the philosophers themselves, constrained by the truth, assert that our Lord God is both invisible and all-powerful. In this matter the eminent Sostenes denies that the form of this [God] can be seen in the world, and says that true angels stand by his throne. With this Plato agrees on the same reasoning, and, proclaiming one God, he calls the others angels or demons. Hermes Trismegistus also acknowledges one God, and confesses him invisible and incomprehensible. This [God], then, we confess in truth, and know, and acknowledge.
passages.notes: 'Sostenes' is probably Ostanes, the Persian magus, as in Minucius Felix; the identification is uncertain. 'formam hujus mundi negat conspici posse' is ambiguous; it may mean 'denies that the form [of God] can be seen in this world'. Scanning errors corrected: velint nolint, invisibilem, confitetur. The marginal number 730 is omitted.

passages.original: Et Verbum caro factum est, et habitavit in nobis (loan. I), quique dicebat: Hcec est vita aeterna, ut cognoscant te solum verum Deum, et quem misisti Jesum Christum (Joan. XVII). Iste Jesus Christus .... in principio erat Verbum apud Deum... a Sibylla ΙΧΘΥΣ, Græco nomine, quod significat piscis, operatus est, eo quod mundi vel sæcult hujus mare ingressurus esset. Nam et litterarum ipsarum Græcarum considera ingens mysterium ΙΧΘΥΣ: I iota, hoc est Jesus; x chi, id est X pios ; Θ theta, Theu;
passages.english: "And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us" (John 1), [he] who also said: "This is eternal life, that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent" (John 17). This Jesus Christus .... in the beginning was the Word with God... was called by the Sibyl ΙΧΘΥΣ, a Greek name, which means "fish", because he was to enter the sea of this world or age. For consider also the great mystery of the Greek letters themselves, ΙΧΘΥΣ: I, iota, that is Jesus [Iēsous]; X, chi, that is Christos; Θ, theta, Theou [of God];
passages.notes: Lacunae in the text. 'operatus est' makes no sense here, and 'vocatus est' (was called) is assumed. 'X pios' is read as Christos and 'Theu' as Theou.
